title: TIDE: Asymmetric Neural Circuits for Stabilized Temporal Inhibitory-Excitatory Dynamics
claim: Each component of the baseline architecture is replaced, modified, extended or newly added in ours, shown stage by stage.
layout: 2 rows (CTM top, TIDE bottom), 9 aligned columns, edit-operation labels between
description: A wide grid compares two architectures. The top row, labeled CTM, has nine gray boxes: Feature Extractor, Neuron Interaction, NLM, Normalize, Synchronize, Cross-attention, Lateral Inhibition, Memory and Output Head. Section references sit above the boxes. Lateral Inhibition and Memory are dashed boxes marked "absent". Tensor shapes sit below the top row. Operation labels between the rows (REPLACE, DUPLICATE, MODIFY, DECOMPOSE, ADD, EXTEND) tell the reader what changed, with dotted vertical lines linking the columns. The bottom row, labeled TIDE, shows the replacement modules in color: green for the conv net and deep HRF, blue and red for the excitatory and inhibitory populations, purple for sync and norm, orange for lateral inhibition, and lime for surprise-gated memory. Tensor shapes appear beneath. The eye goes first to the colored TIDE row.
caption: Schematic architectural comparison between CTM and TIDE. TIDE's architectural components are further described in Section [ref]; Appendix [ref] provides additional technical details.
abstract: Recent Continuous Thought Machine (CTM) architecture decouples internal computation from external inputs via neural dynamics, but relies on unconstrained multi-layer perceptrons for its recurrent computations. We propose to model neural dynamics using asymmetric Excitatory-Inhibitory (E-I) networks, which can be stabilized via principles from network theory, while obeying Dale's principle and can be expressed as energy-based systems optimized through a game-theoretic loss. Building on this perspective, we introduce Temporal Inhibitory-Excitatory Dynamic Engine (TIDE), a neuro-inspired architecture that computes internal representations through neural dynamics stabilized by incorporating the Wilson-Cowan dynamics and lateral inhibition. TIDE balances biological realism by, for instance, using Hierarchical Receptive Fields and enforcing Dale's principle to ensure a realistic $80:20$ E-I balance ratio with an end-to-end trainable architecture. The aim of this paper is to introduce a new architecture that brings neuro-inspired learning and architectural principles to the forefront. We present proofs of convergence, stability, and complexity bounds, along with empirical ablation studies. Overall, TIDE achieves higher $\texttt{top-1}$ accuracy than CTM on the majority of the investigated datasets while requiring a smaller training budget. Furthermore, across varying training budgets, TIDE improves $\texttt{top-1}$ accuracy on ImageNet-C by an average of $+1.65$% to $+6.42$% under different perturbation severity levels.
